findings.claim: The one-glance surface reports a green all-clear on a wedged execution. `status` for exec-m06-dogfood returns status="running", untriagedInterruptions=[], nodeStateCounts={running:1,succeeded:2} — while the event log shows node `judge` in a crash-loop: started → retryable_failure → blocked, rescued by owner approval five separate times (sequences 25/26, 38/39, 45/46, 52/53, 59/60) across 00:51–01:04 with zero forward progress. An operator who glances and goes back to sleep sleeps through a fully stalled graph, which is the exact failure the story exists to prevent.
findings.remediation: Make `status` answer the sleep question directly: add a top-level verdict field (e.g. attentionRequired: bool + reason) that is true whenever any node has entered `blocked`, whenever a node has been re-approved after failure more than once, or whenever the head has not advanced past retry churn. Never let a repeatedly-blocked node be summarized as "running".

findings.claim: `nodeStateCounts` has no failure dimension. It emitted only {running, succeeded} even at moments when `judge` was in state `blocked` (sequences 45, 52, 59). Failure and blocked states are structurally absent from the glance, so the summary cannot express bad news at all.
findings.remediation: Emit every lifecycle state as a bucket, including zero-valued ones: blocked, failed, retrying, queued, paused, awaiting_approval. Zero-fill so the operator can see the bucket exists and is empty rather than inferring absence.

findings.claim: `retryable_failure` events carry no cause. Every judge failure event (sequences 16, 21, 23, 32, 34, 36, 38, 45, 52, 59) has empty evidenceRefs, no error string, no exit code, and no message — while the *succeeded* events do attach stdout/stderr/record evidence. Even after abandoning the glance and reading all 66 events, the operator still cannot tell why judge fails, so they cannot decide whether it is safe to sleep.
findings.remediation: Attach a failure reason and evidenceRefs (stderr/record) to retryable_failure and blocked outcomes with at least the same fidelity as success outcomes, and surface the most recent failure reason as a `lastError` field on `status`.

findings.claim: `wake_status` cannot tell the operator whether their alarm already went off. It returns only {cursor, live, rendezvousId, sessionId} — no head sequence, no fired/consumed flag, no armedAt, no expiry. After arming at cursor 65 when head was already 66, it still reported live:true with nothing indicating the log had moved past the cursor. "Am I safely asleep or did I already miss the ring?" is unanswerable without separately calling `status` and diffing sequence numbers by hand.
findings.remediation: Include headSequence, a fired/pending state, lag (head − cursor), and lease expiry in the wake_status payload; return an explicit `stale: true` when head has advanced past the armed cursor.

findings.claim: Arming the wake lease appends its own event to the stream the lease watches. The wake_arm call wrote sequence 66 (kind wake_lease) to exec-m06-dogfood, advancing head from 65 to 66 as a direct side effect of arming. Arming at head therefore self-invalidates, and a content-free ring cannot be distinguished from the operator's own bookkeeping append.
findings.remediation: Either write lease bookkeeping to a side channel outside the watched stream, or exclude self-authored wake_lease events from ring evaluation, and have wake_arm return the post-append head it actually armed against.

findings.claim: The activity counters on `status` are wrong, and they are wrong in the direction that induces sleep. acceptedMutations=0 and signalsRecorded=0 across two separate reads (head 65 and head 66), despite the log containing five owner approvals plus six pause/resume pairs — all owner-actor mutations. An operator reading "0 mutations" concludes nothing has happened when in fact a human has been repeatedly hand-rescuing a failing node.
findings.remediation: Fix the counters to include owner-actor mutations (approve/pause/resume/signal), or remove them; a silently-zero counter on a monitor is worse than an absent one.

findings.claim: No time or staleness anywhere in `status`. There is no lastEventAt, no startedAt, no time-in-current-state. "running" reads identically for a healthy node one second in and a node wedged for hours; the only way to gauge liveness was to page the event log and diff occurredAt timestamps manually.
findings.remediation: Add lastEventAt, currentStateSince, and an idle/stall threshold flag to `status` so freshness is part of the single glance.

findings.claim: Retry budget and loop detection are invisible. `judge` exhausted its retries into `blocked` on five distinct occasions and each rescue re-entered the same failure path within ~1 second of resuming. Nothing in the surface exposes attempts used, attempts remaining, or the fact that the same node keeps re-blocking — so the operator has no way to see that approving again is futile.
findings.remediation: Expose per-node attempt counts and remaining retry budget, and raise a distinct loop-detected condition when a node re-enters blocked after approval more than once.

findings.claim: Gateway health contradicts observed reality without reconciliation. `probe` on judge_route reports health="available" with runtime check ok, while the node that depends on that route has failed every single attempt. A green dependency panel next to a silently failing consumer actively points triage in the wrong direction.
findings.remediation: Correlate route health with recent consumer outcomes — degrade or annotate a route whose dependent nodes are failing at a high rate, and expose the failing node's route attribution so probe and node state can be cross-read.

findings.claim: The glance is not a glance. Reaching a defensible "can I sleep?" answer took eight tool calls (status, events ×3 to page 66 entries, wake_arm, wake_status, probe, status) plus manual timestamp and sequence arithmetic. Par for this story is one call returning one answer.
findings.remediation: Provide a single sleep-verdict response — a boolean plus a one-line reason plus the top offending node — computable from one call, with the event log reserved for drill-down after the verdict says to wake up.
